units.title: How We Know the Past
units.blurb: Detectives of the past: sources, archaeology, and counting years with BC and AD.

units.title: First Farmers and First Cities
units.blurb: From hunting and gathering to farming villages, then the first cities, writing and laws in Mesopotamia.

units.title: River Kingdoms
units.blurb: Ancient Egypt on the Nile, the cities of the Indus Valley, and the first dynasties of China.

units.title: Greece and Rome
units.blurb: Athens and Sparta, the great Greek thinkers and Alexander, and Rome from a republic to an empire.

units.title: Faiths of the Ancient World
units.blurb: What Jews, Hindus, Buddhists and Christians believe, and how these faiths began and spread.

units.title: The Middle Ages Around the World
units.blurb: Byzantium and the rise of Islam, castles and monasteries, Vikings, China and Japan, the kingdoms of Africa, and the Maya, Aztecs and Incas.

units.title: Renaissance and Exploration
units.blurb: A rebirth of art and learning, the printing press and the Reformation, and voyages across the oceans.

units.title: Revolutions
units.blurb: New ways of doing science, and revolutions in America and France.

units.title: Inventions and the Modern Age
units.blurb: Steam and factories, the long fight to end slavery, an age of inventions, two world wars, and the world from 1945 to 2000.

topics.title: History Detectives
topics.short: We learn about the past from sources: things people made and left behind, and words they wrote. Archaeologists dig them up; historians read and compare them.
topics.trouble: Children think a book about the past is as good as a letter written at the time. A primary source comes from the time itself; a secondary source is written later by someone studying it. Both help, in different ways.

topics.title: Counting the Years: BC and AD
topics.short: Years before the birth of Jesus are counted backward and marked BC; years after are counted forward and marked AD. There is no year 0: 1 BC is followed by AD 1.
topics.trouble: Children read 500 BC as later than 300 BC because 500 is bigger. BC years count down toward AD 1, so 500 BC is earlier. To find years between a BC date and an AD date, add them and take away 1 (there is no year 0).

topics.title: The First Farmers
topics.short: For most of the human story, people hunted animals and gathered wild plants. About 12,000 years ago, people in the Middle East began to plant seeds and tame animals, and villages grew.
topics.trouble: Children picture cavemen living next to dinosaurs. The last big dinosaurs died out about 66 million years before the first people.

topics.title: Mesopotamia: Cities, Writing and Laws
topics.short: Between the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers, the Sumerians built the first cities, invented writing on clay tablets (cuneiform) and used the wheel. King Hammurabi of Babylon wrote down a famous set of laws.
topics.trouble: Children think writing began with letters like ours. The first writing was wedge-shaped marks pressed into wet clay, used first for counting grain and animals.

topics.title: Ancient Egypt: Gift of the Nile
topics.short: The Nile flooded each year and left rich soil, so Egypt could grow plenty of food. Pharaohs ruled for about 3,000 years; Egyptians built pyramids, wrote in hieroglyphs and made mummies.
topics.trouble: Children think all pyramids were built at the same time as Cleopatra. The Great Pyramid is about 2,500 years older than Cleopatra: she lived closer in time to us than to its builders.

topics.title: The Indus Valley and Ancient India
topics.short: Along the Indus River, people built planned cities such as Mohenjo-daro with straight streets and drains. Later, the emperor Ashoka ruled much of India and carved messages of kindness on stone pillars.
topics.trouble: Children assume we can read every ancient script. Nobody can yet read the Indus script; we learn about those cities from what archaeologists dig up.

topics.title: Ancient China: Dynasties, the Great Wall and Silk
topics.short: China's history is counted in dynasties, ruling families. The Shang wrote on bones; Confucius taught about respect and good government; the first emperor joined walls together; the Han traded silk on the Silk Road and made paper.
topics.trouble: Children think the Great Wall was built all at once. It was built and rebuilt over about 2,000 years, by many dynasties; most of what visitors see today was built during the Ming dynasty, after AD 1368.

topics.title: Athens and Sparta
topics.short: Ancient Greece was made of city-states. In Athens, citizens voted on laws themselves, the first democracy. Sparta trained its boys to be soldiers. Together they turned back the Persians.
topics.trouble: Children think everyone in Athens could vote. Only free men born to Athenian parents could; women, enslaved people and foreigners could not. It was still a big new idea: ordinary citizens deciding together.

topics.title: Greek Thinkers and Alexander the Great
topics.short: Socrates asked questions, Plato wrote them down, and Aristotle studied almost everything. Aristotle taught Alexander, who built a huge empire and spread Greek ideas as far as India.
topics.trouble: Children mix up the three thinkers. Teacher to student: Socrates taught Plato, Plato taught Aristotle, Aristotle taught Alexander.

topics.title: Rome: From a Village to a Republic
topics.short: Legend says Romulus founded Rome in 753 BC. In 509 BC the Romans sent away their king and made a republic, where elected leaders and a senate governed. Rome slowly took over Italy and the lands around the Mediterranean.
topics.trouble: Children think a republic and a democracy are the same thing. In a republic people elect leaders to make decisions for them; in Athens, citizens voted on laws themselves.

topics.title: The Roman Empire
topics.short: In 27 BC Augustus became the first Roman emperor. For about 200 years the empire was mostly at peace. Romans built roads, aqueducts and arches, and their language, Latin, lives on in many words we use.
topics.trouble: Children think Julius Caesar was the first emperor. Caesar ruled as dictator and was killed in 44 BC; his adopted son Octavian became the first emperor, Augustus.

topics.title: Judaism, Hinduism and Buddhism
topics.short: Three of the world's oldest faiths: Jews worship one God and follow the Torah; Hindus follow ancient teachings from India called the Vedas; Buddhists follow the teachings of the Buddha about ending suffering.
topics.trouble: Children may treat other people's beliefs as stories that are simply true or false. Here we describe what each faith's followers believe, in their own words, with respect.

topics.title: The Beginning of Christianity
topics.short: Jesus of Nazareth taught in Judea about 2,000 years ago. Christians believe he is the Son of God, who died and rose again. His followers spread the faith around the Roman Empire, and in time it became the empire's main religion.
topics.trouble: Children expect that the BC/AD count was used at the time of Jesus. It was worked out about 500 years later, by a monk named Dionysius Exiguus.

topics.title: Rome Falls in the West, Byzantium Lives On
topics.short: The Western Roman Empire ended in AD 476. The eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, lasted almost 1,000 years more as the Byzantine Empire, with its great church, the Hagia Sophia, and the laws of Justinian.
topics.trouble: Children think all of Rome ended in 476. Only the western half did; the eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire lasted until AD 1453.

topics.title: The Rise of Islam and a Golden Age of Learning
topics.short: Muslims believe that God sent messages to Muhammad, beginning about AD 610, and that the Quran holds those messages. Islam spread quickly, and cities such as Baghdad and Córdoba became centers of science, medicine and books.
topics.trouble: Children think the numerals 0 to 9 are Roman. Our numerals began in India; scholars in Baghdad wrote about them and they reached Europe through the Arab world, so we call them Hindu-Arabic numerals.

topics.title: Castles, Knights and Monasteries
topics.short: In medieval Europe, kings gave land to lords, who were protected by knights and fed by peasants who farmed the land. Monks in monasteries copied books by hand. Charlemagne, crowned emperor in AD 800, encouraged schools.
topics.trouble: Children picture everyone in the Middle Ages as a knight or a princess. Most people were peasants who farmed.

topics.title: The Vikings
topics.short: From Scandinavia, Viking sailors raided, traded and settled across Europe in fast longships. They settled Iceland and Greenland, and about AD 1000 Leif Erikson reached North America.
topics.trouble: Children picture Vikings in horned helmets. No Viking helmet with horns has been found; the horns come from costumes made in the 1800s.

topics.title: Inventions of China and the Samurai of Japan
topics.short: Under the Tang and Song dynasties, China invented or improved printing, gunpowder, the magnetic compass and paper money. In Japan, an emperor reigned, while from 1192 shoguns and their samurai warriors held power.
topics.trouble: Children think the compass, printing and paper were invented in Europe. Paper, woodblock printing and the magnetic compass came from China first.

topics.title: Kingdoms of Africa
topics.short: Africa had rich kingdoms: Aksum in the east, Ghana and Mali in the west, where gold was traded for salt, and Great Zimbabwe in the south. Mansa Musa of Mali was one of the richest rulers who ever lived.
topics.trouble: Children think salt is cheap everywhere. In the Sahara trade, salt was so needed and so scarce in the south that it was traded for gold.

topics.title: The Maya, the Aztecs and the Incas
topics.short: In the Americas, the Maya built stone cities and wrote in glyphs; the Aztecs built Tenochtitlan on a lake; the Incas ran a mountain empire joined by thousands of miles of roads.
topics.trouble: Children think the Maya, Aztecs and Incas lived at the same time in the same place. The Maya cities were greatest about AD 250 to 900 in Central America; the Aztecs (Mexico) and Incas (the Andes) rose in the 1400s.

topics.title: The Renaissance
topics.short: Renaissance means rebirth. Beginning in Italian cities such as Florence in the 1400s, artists and scholars studied the books and art of Greece and Rome and made new art, like Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo.
topics.trouble: Children think Leonardo da Vinci was only a painter. He also filled notebooks with studies of birds, water, machines and the human body.

topics.title: The Printing Press and the Reformation
topics.short: About 1450, Johannes Gutenberg printed books with movable metal type. Books became cheaper and ideas spread fast. In 1517 Martin Luther's writings began the Reformation, which divided Western Christians into Catholics and Protestants.
topics.trouble: Children think Gutenberg invented printing. Woodblock printing and even movable type were used earlier in China and Korea; Gutenberg made a fast metal-type press that worked well with European alphabets.

topics.title: The Age of Exploration
topics.short: Sailors crossed the oceans: Zheng He sailed from China to Africa, Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492, and Magellan's crew sailed all the way around the world. Plants, animals and diseases crossed with them.
topics.trouble: Children think Columbus proved the Earth was round. Educated Europeans already knew it was round; Columbus thought the Earth was smaller than it is and that Asia was close.

topics.title: The Scientific Revolution
topics.short: Copernicus said the Earth goes around the Sun; Galileo looked through a telescope and saw moons circling Jupiter; Newton explained gravity. People began testing ideas with careful experiments.
topics.trouble: Children think Galileo invented the telescope. The telescope was first made in the Netherlands in 1608; Galileo built better ones and was among the first to turn them to the sky.

topics.title: The American Revolution
topics.short: Thirteen British colonies in North America declared independence on July 4, 1776, won the war, and wrote the Constitution in 1787. George Washington became the first president.
topics.trouble: Children think the war ended in 1776. The Declaration was signed in 1776; the war went on until 1783.

topics.title: The French Revolution and Napoleon
topics.short: In 1789 the people of France rose up against their king, demanding "liberty, equality, fraternity." The revolution brought new rights and a time of fear and war; then Napoleon made himself emperor, until his defeat at Waterloo in 1815.
topics.trouble: Children think Napoleon was very short. He was about average height for his time; the idea partly comes from a mix-up between French and English inches and from cartoons by his enemies.

topics.title: Steam and Factories: The Industrial Revolution
topics.short: Beginning in Britain in the 1700s, machines driven by water and steam began to do work once done by hand. Factories, railways and big cities grew, and so did new problems, like children working long hours.
topics.trouble: Children think James Watt invented the steam engine. Engines like Thomas Newcomen's pumped water from mines earlier; Watt made a much better one.

topics.title: The Long Fight to End Slavery
topics.short: Slavery is very old, but in the 1700s and 1800s people began to fight to end it. Britain ended its slave trade in 1807 and slavery in most of its empire in the 1830s; the United States ended slavery in 1865.
topics.trouble: Children think slavery ended everywhere at once. It ended at different times in different countries: Britain's empire in the 1830s, the United States in 1865, Brazil in 1888.

topics.title: An Age of Inventions
topics.short: In about 100 years, inventors gave the world the telegraph, the telephone, the electric light, the car and the airplane. Marie Curie discovered new elements and won two Nobel Prizes.
topics.trouble: Children think Edison invented the light bulb from nothing. Many people made glowing lamps before him; Edison and his team made a long-lasting bulb and a system to bring electricity to homes.

topics.title: Two World Wars
topics.short: Two terrible wars were fought by many nations: World War I (1914 to 1918) and World War II (1939 to 1945). Afterward, countries formed the United Nations to try to keep the peace.
topics.trouble: Children mix up which war came first or think they were the same war. World War I ended in 1918; World War II began 21 years later, in 1939.

topics.title: The World from 1945 to 2000
topics.short: After World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union competed in a long Cold War and a race to space; people walked on the Moon in 1969. The Berlin Wall fell in 1989, and computers and the World Wide Web changed daily life.
topics.trouble: Children think the Cold War had big battles between the United States and the Soviet Union. The two never fought each other directly; they competed with weapons, spies, space rockets and allies.
